content: Crunchbase News https://news.crunchbase.com/ Data-driven reporting on private markets, startups, founders, and investors Wed, 18 Nov 2026 22:15:36 +0000 en-US hourly 1 https://wordpress.org/?v=6.8.12 https://news.crunchbase.com/wp-content/uploads/cb_news_favicon-150x150.png Crunchbase News https://news.crunchbase.com/ 32 32 Anthropic Prices IPO Shares At $83, Above Range https://news.crunchbase.com/public/ipo/anthropic-prices-ipo-ant-above-range/ Wed, 18 Nov 2026 22:15:36 +0000 https://news.crunchbase.com/?p=94423 Anthropic priced shares for its upcoming stock market debut at $83 on Wednesday afternoon, solidly above the expected range of $70 to $78 laid out in its IPO filing, CNBC, Reuters and the Wall Street Journal reported, citing sources familiar with the matter. The offering promises to be the public market event of the season, with the Claude creator seeing investor demand for shares well in excess of its capital-raising goals. The stock is slated to begin trading Thursday on Nasdaq under the ticker symbol ANT. For the IPO portion of its fundraise, Anthropic plans to sell just over 800 million shares, bringing in about $66.4 billion. Anthropic also expects to pull in another $26 billion from a private placement slated to close immediately following the IPO. Investors in this include AMD , Broadcom , Google , Micron Technology , Microsoft , Nvidia and TSMC . Put together, the IPO and private placement total more than $92 billion. It’s a record-setting capital haul for a company making its market debut. SpaceX , by comparison, raised $75 billion in its June offering. Fast growth but no profits, yet The IPO follows a revenue growth trajectory for the history books. For the first nine months of the year, the company had $33.2 billion in revenue, up from $2.5 billion in the same period a year ago. Anthropic claims it has the fastest enterprise adoption of any technology to date, growing revenue from zero at commercial launch in the first quarter of 2023 to $17 billion for the three months ended Sept. 30, 2026. As of yet, however, it’s not profitable. Anthropic posted an operating loss of $1.3 billion for the first nine months of the year, down from $5.2 billion a year earlier. Its net loss widened to $104 billion, up from $25.1 billion a year ago. The San Francisco-based company also presents a stark contrast to the more common theme in recent years of venture-backed companies staying private longer: Anthropic is less than six years old as it goes public in a potentially record-setting listing. Those metrics are impressive, but there are other numbers in its S-1 I keep circling, too, like the nearly $900 billion in compute purchase and lease commitments. I’ve worked in Silicon Valley through the dot-com boom and bust, the rise of SaaS, social media, unicorn and decacorn startups and now, AI. Anthropic’s extraordinary rise and entrance onto the public markets marks a new technology era — one with enormous growth and potential, but also tremendous costs, risks and unknowns. OpenAI ’s seminal success was the launch of chatbots in 2022 — within two months, ChatGPT reached 100 million users and in less than four years, OpenAI had a billion monthly active users. By contrast, Anthropic’s breakout was the success of Claude Code, launched just last year. Already, Anthropic says 11,900 companies use the product, spending $100,000 or more trailing 12 months, up 12x from a year ago. In its S-1 , the company says that marks the fastest enterprise adoption for any company on record. Anthropic’s IPO could value it at $1.4 trillion and raise $88.5 billion via the IPO and concurrent private placement. As it becomes public, I’ll be watching closely to see if the company can keep turning demand for Claude and Claude Code into a durable business while building out the astounding amount of compute it says it needs and managing the many risks that surround its technology. By the numbers Here are some of the other key details and figures that caught my eye ahead of Anthropic’s first day on the public markets: The company has a purchase and lease agreement for $895.4 billion for compute. Of that, $447.5 billion will be incurred before the end of 2030. Anthropic currently has over $100 billion on its balance sheet. Its IPO seeks to add another roughly $100 billion, creating a war chest for those compute commitments. When it launched Claude in the first quarter of 2023, Anthropic had zero revenue. In less than four years, revenue reached $17 billion in Q3 2026, up 12x from Q3 2025. More than 1,900 customers spend more than $1 million and 250 more than $10 million, trailing 12 months, according to the company. Its per-employee revenue figures are impressive: Each employee supports $6.6 million in trailing 12-month revenue as of Sept 30, 2026. Anthropic is putting aside 5% of equity for a fund devoted to public good, adding 2% for every 50% increase in share price. Each founder is selling roughly $250 million worth of shares in the listing, depending on its final listing price. The backers behind Anthropic’s rise Anthropic got to where it is now through a fast sequence of funding rounds, from its Jaan Tallinn -led Series A in 2021 to its Series H in May of this year that valued the company at $965 billion. Other lead investors over its many funding rounds include Google , Amazon , Spark Capital , Menlo Ventures , Lightspeed Venture Partners , Coatue and Sequoia Capital, all of whom are slated to be among the winners when it goes public tomorrow. Risks, opportunities and what’s ahead The AI era has the potential to generate massive amounts of new wealth and unlock life-changing technological advances. But it also comes with huge risks. Anthropic’s S-1 captures that tension. The opportunity the company describes extends far beyond coding and software. It says its focus in 2027 will be AI agents for knowledge work and scientific discovery. It also points to potential gains in biology and rare-disease research, economic growth, wider access to health care and improved government services. The S-1 cites the World Health Organization ’s estimate that 4.6 billion people lack access to basic health services. That promise comes with a competitive risk for its customers, too: Companies may worry that data they share with AI providers could help train models that compete with their products, or that more capable models could erode parts of their existing businesses. Anthropic’s S-1 also flags risks ranging from cyber and biological attacks to unpredictable model behavior, authoritarian surveillance and economic disruption. Anthropic’s public-benefit structure is meant to balance those competing pressures. As a public benefit corporation, the company says it must weigh commercial success against the public good. Its founders, employees and Long-Term Benefit Trust share in governance; the trust has no financial stake and weighs impacts on national security, economics, global health and science.
